header.title: Reproductive Anatomy
header.subtitle: Female and male reproductive anatomy in dogs and cats, the four-phase estrous cycle, and clinical connections to breeding soundness, pregnancy, and reproductive health examinations.

quiz.q: Which structure connects each ovary to the uterine horn and is the normal site of fertilization?
quiz.exp: The uterine tube (oviduct) connects the ovary to the uterine horn and is where fertilization normally occurs.

quiz.q: True or False: Dogs and cats have a single, undivided uterus, so a pregnancy can only be located in one central chamber.
quiz.exp: False. Dogs and cats have a bicornuate uterus with two uterine horns, and pregnancies implant along both horns.

quiz.q: Which structure stays closed except around estrus and parturition, and is a key landmark during a vaginal exam?
quiz.exp: The cervix is a firm, muscular landmark that remains closed except around estrus and parturition.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the PetNurse's role during a female reproductive exam?
quiz.exp: Female reproductive exams are performed by the attending DVM. The PetNurse supports positioning, comfort, and accurate documentation.
opts: The PetNurse performs the vaginal exam independently.
The PetNurse supports positioning and comfort while the DVM performs the exam, and helps ensure accurate Hannahware documentation.
The PetNurse interprets ultrasound findings for the Member.
The PetNurse decides whether the patient is pregnant.

modules.title: Female Reproductive Anatomy
modules.content:
The female reproductive tract in dogs and cats is built around a pair of ovaries, which produce oocytes and the hormones that drive the estrous cycle. Each ovary connects to a short, coiled uterine tube (oviduct), where fertilization occurs before the embryo travels into the uterus.

Dogs and cats have a bicornuate uterus: two long uterine horns extend from each side and join in the midline at a short uterine body before narrowing into the cervix, a firm, muscular landmark that stays closed except around estrus and parturition. Litters typically implant along both horns rather than in a single central chamber, which is why palpation and ultrasound scan the full length of each horn.

Past the cervix, the vagina forms the birth canal and the site of natural mating and vaginal cytology sampling. The tract ends externally at the vulva, the visible landmark PetNurses reference when describing discharge, swelling, or discomfort in the medical record.

Clinical connection: Female reproductive exams may include external observation of the vulva, a vaginal exam, rectal palpation, or ultrasound to assess estrus stage, pregnancy, uterine health, or ovarian structures. These exams are performed by the attending DVM. The PetNurse's role is to support safe positioning and patient comfort, communicate what's happening to the Member in plain, non-diagnostic language, and use accurate terminology so the Nurse Aide can document findings in Hannahware in real time.

quiz.q: Which structure produces sperm and testosterone?
quiz.exp: The testis produces both sperm and testosterone.

quiz.q: Where does sperm mature and get stored before ejaculation?
quiz.exp: Sperm matures and is stored along the epididymis before traveling through the vas deferens.

quiz.q: True or False: Cats have an os penis, just like dogs.
quiz.exp: False. Dogs have an os penis that supports the urethra; cats do not.

quiz.q: Which two assessments are part of a breeding-soundness evaluation, according to this lesson?
quiz.exp: A breeding-soundness evaluation combines a physical exam, scrotal circumference measurement, and semen evaluation.
opts: Scrotal circumference measurement and semen evaluation

modules.title: Male Reproductive Anatomy
modules.content:
The male reproductive tract starts with a pair of testes, which produce sperm and testosterone. Each testis sits inside the scrotum, an external sac that helps regulate testicular temperature — a detail that matters clinically, since retained (undescended) testes can't cool properly and carry a higher risk of testicular tumors.

Sperm matures and is stored along the epididymis, a coiled structure on the surface of the testis, before traveling through the vas (ductus) deferens toward the pelvis. Along the way, accessory sex glands add secretions to the ejaculate; the prostate gland is the primary accessory gland in male dogs and surrounds the urethra near the bladder neck, while cats have a smaller prostate and add bulbourethral gland secretions.

The penis is the copulatory and urination organ, covered and protected by a skin fold called the prepuce. Dogs have a bone called the os penis that supports the urethra — a detail worth knowing, since it can complicate urinary catheterization or obstruction cases. Cats do not have an os penis.

Clinical connection: A breeding-soundness evaluation combines a physical exam, scrotal circumference measurement, and semen evaluation. PetNurses may assist with restraint, patient comfort, and Hannahware documentation while the attending DVM performs the physical exam and any sample collection.

quiz.q: Which phase of the canine estrous cycle is marked by the LH surge that triggers ovulation?
quiz.exp: Estrus is when estrogen peaks, the female is receptive to breeding, and the LH surge triggers ovulation.

quiz.q: During which phase does the corpus luteum form and progesterone begin rising?
quiz.exp: Metestrus follows ovulation: the corpus luteum forms and progesterone begins rising.

quiz.q: True or False: Cats are induced ovulators, meaning ovulation is normally triggered by mating rather than occurring spontaneously.
quiz.exp: True. Cats are seasonally polyestrous, induced ovulators — mating typically triggers the LH surge that causes ovulation.

quiz.q: Which hormone dominates during diestrus and supports pregnancy if it occurred?
quiz.exp: Progesterone, produced by the corpus luteum, dominates during diestrus and supports pregnancy.

modules.title: Reproductive Physiology & the Estrous Cycle
modules.content:
The estrous cycle is the hormonal cycle that governs fertility in female dogs and cats. In dogs, it runs through four phases in order, driven by shifting levels of estrogen, luteinizing hormone (LH), and progesterone:

  • Proestrus — ovarian follicles develop and estrogen rises; the Member may notice swelling and bloody discharge, but the female is not yet receptive to breeding.
  • Estrus — estrogen peaks, the female becomes receptive to breeding, and a surge in luteinizing hormone (LH) triggers ovulation.
  • Metestrus — ovulation has occurred; the corpus luteum forms on the ovary and progesterone begins rising.
  • Diestrus — the corpus luteum is active and progesterone dominates, supporting pregnancy if it occurred; if not, the cycle resets after the corpus luteum regresses.

Between cycles, dogs enter anestrus, a quiescent period with minimal reproductive hormone activity before the next proestrus begins.

Species note: cats follow a different pattern. Cats are seasonally polyestrous, induced ovulators — the LH surge that triggers ovulation is normally stimulated by mating rather than occurring automatically. Without that stimulus, a queen can cycle repeatedly through proestrus and estrus without ovulating.

Clinical connection: Recognizing cycle stage matters for spay timing, pregnancy diagnosis timing, and interpreting a Member's description of heat symptoms. PetNurses use this vocabulary daily when documenting history in Hannahware and relaying accurate, non-diagnostic information to Members.

overview.intro: Spay and neuter surgical prep, pregnancy checks, dystocia calls, and breeding-soundness conversations all start with the same vocabulary. This lesson builds a working map of female and male reproductive anatomy in dogs and cats, then connects it to the estrous cycle and the exams PetNurses support every day.
